quick.summary: Why color alone fails users, and how to add a second signal.
quick.takeaway: Always add an icon or text label alongside color changes.

beats.line: A user deleted their file by mistake. Is my bright green button not obvious?
Think of a traffic light. With the sun in your eyes, can you tell?
No, it just looks washed out.
Right. Your user might be outside, or using a dim screen.
We call this a situational visual impairment.
Can I just say bad lighting?
You can. We all lose our best vision sometimes.
So color alone is not enough to guide them.
Never rely on color alone to give a warning or show a state.
Then how do I make the warning completely clear?
Your user cannot see the bright red color of your delete button.
I need to give a second signal. Like the position of a traffic light.
Exactly. In an interface, that means adding shapes or words.
Do not just make the error text red.
I should add a warning icon next to the text.
Yes. A heavy outline or a clear icon works instantly.
And for buttons, I can add a text label next to the icon.
Words are the safest fallback of all.
I use color, but I add an icon or label to be absolutely sure.
You give every user two ways to understand it.

quiz.question: How can you ensure a critical error message is noticed in bad lighting?
options: Use a heavy icon next to the text.
Make the text a brighter red.
Move it to the top of the screen.
quiz.explanation: If lighting or vision prevents someone from seeing the red color, the icon provides a reliable second signal.

quiz.question: Situational visual impairment only affects people with permanent vision loss.
quiz.explanation: Anyone can experience situational impairment, like trying to read a screen with the sun shining directly on it.
